entry.title: Hypothesis Testing with a Terminal Illness

link.title: Hypothesis Testing with a Terminal Illness

entry.content:
My dad was diagnosed with glioblastoma in April 2026, and he died later that year. I spent those months as his advocate and medical liaison, and I approached the job the way I approach everything, as a scientist. I read the papers, learned the vocabulary, and wrote to clinical trial coordinators. I believed that if I understood the evidence well enough, we could make good decisions.

After his surgery, we were urged to do a six-week course of radiation, and we were promised he would bounce back afterward. He did not. He declined quickly, and we spent the rest of the summer not knowing whether the tumors had shrunk or grown. On an MRI, a growing tumor and a brain reacting to radiation can look alike, so each scan handed us a new question where we had hoped for an answer.

I think about it now as an experiment. The hypothesis was that radiation would shrink the cancer. But the treatment also added a variable. Once he was irradiated, every change in him had two possible causes, the disease and the treatment, and nobody could tease them apart. I would never accept that design in my own work. There was one subject, no control, and an intervention that confounded the only outcome we cared about.

I believe his decline was faster because of the radiation. We gave up good days for a little more time, and we made that trade because the hypothesis had to be tested. It was never presented to us as an experiment. It was presented as the standard of care.

The evidence behind that standard is real. It comes from trials with hundreds of patients, and it says that on average, radiation extends life. But an average answers a question about a population. My family was asking about one man and one summer, and science had no instrument for that. Science failed us. The method worked as designed, and it was not designed for us.
entry.summary: What my dad's glioblastoma taught me about the limits of the scientific method.

entry.title: TLC 2025: Jeff Dozier Snow Study Site

link.title: TLC 2025: Jeff Dozier Snow Study Site

entry.content:
This fall I joined the crew for the 2025 Tender, Loving, Care (TLC) trip to the newly renamed Jeff Dozier Snow Study Site. This is my first field session with Leidos, and the trip was a good introduction. The site has run continuously for 39 years, which makes it one of the longest-running full energy balance snow measurement stations in the world.

We repainted the site and stenciled it with its new name.

Most of my work happens on a screen, and a screen teaches you to expect control. Every part of a pipeline was built by someone, so every part can, in principle, be fixed. That is why a job that fails for no visible reason is so infuriating. It feels like a broken promise. A mountainside makes no such promise. In the field, most of what happens is outside my control, and it ought to be. Accepting that takes a humility I rarely feel at a keyboard, and it was good to feel it again.
entry.summary: Fall maintenance at the Jeff Dozier Snow Study Site with the Leidos snow team.

entry.title: Annual Cropland Extent (ACE)
entry.content:
My main project at Working Lands for Wildlife was the Annual Cropland Extent (ACE) dataset. ACE maps cropland across the central grasslands of North America at 30-meter resolution for every year from 1996 to 2021. The paper is published in Ecological Indicators, and the interactive map is live on Earth Engine.

The core model is an Attention U-Net trained on Landsat composites. For each pixel, it classifies whether the land was actively cultivated in a given year. We ran it across roughly 10 million square kilometers for 26 years, which works out to about 260 million classified square kilometers. After bias correction, the model achieved about 90% accuracy. That is comparable to other cropland products, although I’m still not sure what “accuracy” really means when you evaluate an image model at this scale.

The code is on GitHub if you want to dig into the pipeline. It’s set up for demonstration purposes, but it should give you a good sense of the approach.

entry.title: Landscape Explorer
entry.content:
While I was at Working Lands for Wildlife, I did the data engineering for Landscape Explorer. The tool lets you compare historic aerial imagery (going back to the 1950s) with recent satellite imagery across the western US. WLFW wrote about it here.

Most of the processing happened in Google Earth Engine. Getting decades of imagery into a consistent, servable format was a headache. The projections differed, the metadata was inconsistent, and the coverage had gaps. These are standard problems with historic geospatial data, but they took me a while to work through.

I took two lessons away from this project.

First, design for idempotency. At this scale, batch jobs fail constantly. If your scripts can’t pick up where they left off, you end up re-processing data you have already handled, and that means days of wasted compute.

Second, link each downloading script to its repo. Months later, you will need to trace which script produced which file.

If you want to see how much the West has changed, go poke around at landscapeexplorer.org. The Great Plains conversions are especially striking.

entry.title: Fire Detection: From Research to Operations

link.title: Fire Detection: From Research to Operations

entry.content:
While I was at BAERI on a NASA Ames contract, I built a data fusion framework for satellite-based fire detection. The model combines geostationary imagery with polar-orbiting imagery. Fusing the two lets the model detect fires in near real-time. I also integrated the pipeline with AWS so it could keep up with full-disk geostationary imagery at an operational cadence.

After I moved on, a close friend of mine took the model and built an operational pipeline around it on Google Cloud Platform. Here is how it works:

  • Cloud Functions ingest and reproject the imagery.
  • A containerized Cloud Run instance runs inference. It loads the raster stack, passes it through the PyTorch UNET, and writes the classifications back as a georeferenced band.
  • High-confidence pixels are grouped into fire polygons using connected components.
  • The polygons are uploaded to BigQuery and served to a live map through Flask.

The pipeline is modular. New model weights go in as a .pt file, and a new region of interest goes in as a NetCDF template. The model needs retraining, but the infrastructure is solid. Seeing my research code turn into something operational has been pretty cool, but I can’t take credit for the hard part.

entry.title: How Animals Keep Time
entry.content:
Learning bird calls came easily to me, and I credit that to years of ear training in classical music. Picking out an interval or a rhythm in a practice room is the same work as picking out one singer in a full canopy.

In classical music, rhythm is not a clock. The notes on the page have exact durations, which always exist, but only against the relative timing that a performer has chosen for each part of music. Chopin is said to have taught that the left hand must hold the pulse while the right hand phrases freely against it. The freedom only reads as freedom because a fixed reference sits underneath it. The time taken in one bar is measured against a pulse the listener can still feel.

A forest works in a similar way.

Anyone who has listened deeply outdoors knows that different groups of animals keep different kinds of time.

  • Insects are the percussion and the drone. Crickets and katydids (the Orthoptera) lay down a pulse so steady that it stops sounding like rhythm and starts sounding like texture. Their tempo follows the temperature, and it has nothing to do with mood.
  • Mammals keep a beat. A Red Squirrel scolding from a branch calls at regular intervals, over and over, like a metronome with an opinion.
  • Birds phrase. A thrush sings a line, waits, and sings another, and the waits are never quite the same length. Birds are the right hand.

What strikes me is that none of these players is keeping time for the others, yet the forest seems to have a natural ebb-and-flow. The cricket is not accompanying the thrush. Each one follows its own reasons, and the music is what a listener hears when they overlap. In a concert hall, one performer bends time on purpose to tell a story. In a forest, the bending comes from many separate lives, and the story is whatever the listener can put together.

On stage, listening is intuitive. I hear small differences in my own playing as they happen, react to them, and build the narrative and drama out of them on the fly. Birding by ear asks for the same soft focus, which is what lets a distant, obscure, or uncommon song come through. In both cases I hold a steady pulse in one part of my attention and let another part follow whatever refuses to be steady.
entry.summary: Learning bird calls came easily to me, and I credit that to years of ear training in classical music. Picking out an interval or a rhythm in a practice room is the same work as picking out one singer in a full canopy.

entry.title: Horseshoe Crabs in the Gulf
entry.content:
In the summer of 2015, I was an REU (Research Experience for Undergraduates) student at the Dauphin Island Sea Lab in Alabama. I worked on the population ecology of the American horseshoe crab (Limulus polyphemus) in the northcentral Gulf of Mexico. The paper came out in PLOS ONE in 2021, six years later.

We wanted to know which environmental factors drive horseshoe crab occurrence in this part of the Gulf. We also had a more practical question: can molts and carcasses stand in as indirect indicators of a horseshoe crab population? Direct population surveys are expensive and logistically difficult. If what washes up on shore carries a reliable signal, monitoring becomes much cheaper.

This was my first real research experience. I surveyed beaches, collected and cataloged specimens, and recorded environmental conditions. I also helped develop the research questions and the study design, and I contributed to the analysis of which environmental variables predicted horseshoe crab presence. I presented the work as a poster at the AGU Ocean Sciences Meeting in 2016 in New Orleans.

entry.title: Welcome to Earth to Sean
entry.content:
Welcome to Earth to Sean! This is where I keep my thoughts on science, music, birds, life, and my attempts at Vietnamese in one place.

Why this site?

My professional career and interests are hard to define, but I find that everyone I enjoy working with has a multifaceted and diverse life. If I’m ever looking for new positions, I’d like to be able to show people some more sides of me than what they see during virtual interviews.

I used to spend a lot of energy trying to convince people that my devotion, discipline, and intuition that I built over years of practicing piano was a garden from which any skills can grow. Now, looking backwards, this is definitely true.

My first paying jobs out of college were working maintenance at the Southwestern Research Station and washing dishes at the Portal Peak Cafe. In Portal, I met countless birding fanatics and learned directly from them. That experience was my springboard into field ecology (mostly ornithology), which I eventually worked into a Master’s degree in Systems Ecology. Underneath all of that is my training in classical piano performance. So this site is my attempt to organize the disparate parts of my life, putting the science and the personal side by side to see what happens.

What to expect

I’ll mostly write a bunch of half-baked ideas about music, birding, language, identity, and work. Don’t expect many tutorials. I have much to learn in all of these areas, and most of these posts will be me writing down random thoughts.
entry.summary: First post — why I built this site and what to expect.
